title: Cumulative binomial probabilities
keyIdea: For X ~ B(n, p), a cumulative probability P(X ≤ k) adds up every bar from 0 to k, and it is what tables and calculators give you. Because X takes only whole numbers, translate the words into the exact values first: 'fewer than 6' is X ≤ 5, 'more than 3' is X ≥ 4. Then use the complement for an upper tail, P(X ≥ k) = 1 − P(X ≤ k − 1), and a difference for a range, P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = P(X ≤ b) − P(X ≤ a − 1).
familyTip: Ask your teenager to explain the difference between 'at least 4' and 'more than 4' using a dice game or a number of goals scored. Then ask which they would subtract from 1 to get each one. Saying the values out loud, 4, 5, 6 and so on, catches most mistakes.

visual.caption: X ~ B(12, 0.3). Which expression gives each event? Drag each card, or tap it and then a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: turn words into whole-number values, find tails and ranges from a cumulative chart, drag p and translate real situations.

kid: A binomial count X can only be a whole number: 0, 1, 2 and so on up to n. So the words in a question matter. 'At least 4' keeps 4. 'More than 4' does not. 'Fewer than 6' means up to 5. Write the values out before you do anything else.
A cumulative probability, P(X ≤ k), adds every bar from 0 up to k. Your calculator and the tables give this one. For X ~ B(12, 0.3), P(X ≤ 3) = 0.4925.
For an upper tail, use the complement. Everything adds to 1, so P(X ≥ 4) = 1 − P(X ≤ 3) = 0.5075. Take away only the values you do not want, which stop at 3, not 4.
For a range, subtract two cumulative values. P(3 ≤ X ≤ 7) keeps 3 to 7, so it is P(X ≤ 7) − P(X ≤ 2). You take away up to 2, because 3 is in the range and must stay.
adult: Ages 16 to 18. This is in the A level Mathematics content for England (Statistics: calculate probabilities using the binomial distribution, including cumulative probabilities, using a calculator or tables) and supports later work on hypothesis tests, where critical regions are found from these tails.

Key terms: binomial distribution, X ~ B(n, p), cumulative distribution function P(X ≤ k), complement, upper and lower tail, inclusive and strict inequality, discrete random variable. The lab uses B(12, 0.3), with P(X ≤ 2) = 0.2528, P(X ≤ 3) = 0.4925, P(X ≤ 5) = 0.8822 and P(X ≤ 7) = 0.9905 to 4 decimal places.

Common mistakes, all at the boundaries. Writing P(X ≥ 4) as 1 − P(X ≤ 4). Treating 'fewer than 6' as X ≤ 6. Subtracting P(X ≤ a) instead of P(X ≤ a − 1) for a range, which drops the lowest value. Taking the lower tail when the question asks for the upper one. Students should list the values in words before choosing a calculator function, and check that the answer is between 0 and 1.

practice.prompt: X ~ B(15, 0.4). Which expression gives P(X ≥ 6)?
practice.hint: At least 6 keeps 6. Which values do you not want?
practice.explain: You do not want 0 to 5, so P(X ≥ 6) = 1 − P(X ≤ 5). 1 − P(X ≤ 6) would also remove 6.

practice.prompt: X ~ B(20, p). 'Fewer than {k} successes' is P(X ≤ c). What is c?
practice.hint: Fewer than {k} leaves {k} out. What is the largest whole number kept?
practice.explain: Fewer than {k} means 0 up to {=k-1}, so c = {=k-1}.

practice.prompt: X ~ B(20, p). P(X ≥ {k}) = 1 − P(X ≤ c). What is c?
practice.hint: At least {k} keeps {k}. Take away only the values below it.
practice.explain: The unwanted values are 0 to {=k-1}, so P(X ≥ {k}) = 1 − P(X ≤ {=k-1}).

practice.hint: Keep 3 to 7: subtract the cumulative value just below 3.
practice.explain: P(X ≤ 7) − P(X ≤ 2) = 0.9905 − 0.2528 = 0.7377. A probability over 1 is a sign of adding instead of subtracting.

practice.prompt: X ~ B(10, 0.5). Which expression gives P(2 < X < 7)?
practice.hint: Strict on both sides: list the values kept.
practice.explain: 2 < X < 7 keeps 3, 4, 5, 6, so it is P(X ≤ 6) − P(X ≤ 2).

pool.hint: More than 5 leaves 5 out. It is the complement of X ≤ 5.

pool.prompt: P({a} ≤ X ≤ {b}) = P(X ≤ {b}) − P(X ≤ c). What is c?
pool.hint: The value {a} is in the range. Take away only what is below it.
pool.explain: Values below the range are 0 to {=a-1}, so c = {=a-1}.

pool.prompt: 'No more than 3 faulty' when X counts faulty items is…
pool.hint: No more than 3 means 3 or fewer.
pool.explain: No more than 3 is 0, 1, 2 or 3, so P(X ≤ 3). P(X < 3) leaves 3 out.

pool.prompt: X ~ B(n, p) with n = {n}. 'More than {k}' is X ≥ c. What is c?
pool.hint: More than {k} leaves {k} out, and X is a whole number.
pool.explain: More than {k} means {=k+1} or more, so c = {=k+1}.

pool.prompt: With n = 12 fixed, p rises from 0.3 to 0.5. What happens to P(X ≤ 3)?
pool.hint: A bigger p moves the distribution towards larger counts.
pool.explain: The bars move right, so the lower tail shrinks: P(X ≤ 3) falls from 0.4925 to about 0.0730.

pool.prompt: A student writes P(X ≥ 4) = 1 − P(X ≤ 4). What is the slip?
choices: They have removed 4, which should be kept
pool.hint: List the values in X ≥ 4 and in X ≤ 4. Which value is in both?
pool.explain: 4 is in 'at least 4', so subtract only P(X ≤ 3): P(X ≥ 4) = 1 − P(X ≤ 3).

pool.prompt: X ~ B(12, 0.3), P(X ≤ 0) = 0.0138. Find P(at least one success).
pool.hint: At least one is everything except zero.

pool.prompt: Which is the same as P(X < 9) for a binomial X?
pool.hint: X is a whole number. What is the largest value below 9?
pool.explain: X < 9 means 8 or fewer, so P(X < 9) = P(X ≤ 8).
